answers.core:
Yes, this should be a core feature for several important reasons:
1. Requires Deep Editor Integration
Needs access to the preview/run system that add-ons cannot modify
Requires integration with editor's play button and debug controls
Must hook into the mobile editor's preview pipeline
Needs system-level input routing before it reaches the game
Add-ons cannot access these low-level editor systems.
2. Platform-Specific Implementation
Requires different implementations for Android vs iOS
Needs optimization for mobile-specific constraints (memory, battery, touch input)
Must integrate with mobile OS lifecycle management
Requires platform-specific performance profiling
This level of platform integration is only feasible at the core level.
3. Parity with Desktop Feature
Desktop Godot has "Run Multiple Instances" as a core debug feature
Mobile equivalent should also be core to maintain feature parity
Debug/testing features belong in the editor core, not as add-ons
This is fundamental development tooling, not optional functionality
4. Accessibility Mission
This directly supports Godot's mission of accessible game development
Add-ons create additional barriers (discovery, installation, compatibility)
Mobile-only developers need this built-in, not hidden in asset library
Core features signal official support and maintenance
5. Maintenance and Compatibility
Add-ons break between Godot versions
Core features receive proper testing and updates
Mobile-only developers may not know to look for add-ons
Critical development tools need guaranteed long-term support
6. User Experience
New developers expect basic debugging tools to be built-in
Having to install an add-on for essential multiplayer testing is poor UX
Core integration provides better performance and reliability
Consistent experience across desktop and mobile editors
7. Technical Limitations of Add-ons
Add-ons cannot:
Modify the editor's run/preview system
Add new preview modes to the play button dropdown
Access low-level inp
answers.workaround:
No, this cannot be effectively worked around with a few lines of script.
While technically possible to create SubViewports manually, the workaround requires:
Significant scripting knowledge - Creating viewports, managing input routing, handling touch events per-viewport, setting up proper containers and layouts
30-50+ lines of complex code minimum for basic functionality
Deep understanding of Godot's viewport system, input handling, and scene management
Manual setup for every project - not reusable across projects easily
No debugging tools - developers still can't pause, inspect, or manage individual instances easily
Example of current "workaround" complexity:
# This is the "simple" version - still too complex for many users
extends Control

var viewports = []
var game_scene = preload("res://main.tscn")

func _ready():
    var hsplit = HSplitContainer.new()
    add_child(hsplit)
    
    for i in range(2):
        var viewport = SubViewport.new()
        viewport.size = get_viewport_rect().size / 2
        viewport.render_target_update_mode = SubViewport.UPDATE_ALWAYS
        
        var game = game_scene.instantiate()
        viewport.add_child(game)
        
        var container = SubViewportContainer.new()
        container.stretch = true
        container.add_child(viewport)
        hsplit.add_child(container)
        
        viewports.append(viewport)
    
    hsplit.split_offset = get_viewport_rect().size.x / 2

func _input(event):
    if event is InputEventScreenTouch or event is InputEventScreenDrag:
        var viewport_index = 0 if event.position.x < get_viewport_rect().size.x / 2 else 1
        var local_pos = event.position
        local_pos.x = fmod(local_pos.x, get_viewport_rect().size.x / 2)
        
        var new_event = event.duplicate()
        new_event.position = local_pos
        viewports[viewport_index].push_input(new_event)
        get_viewport().set_input_as_handled()
